column7: Lactase persistence (digesting milk sugar as an adult)
column8: No copy of -13910T, the European lactase persistence allele. In people of European descent lactase activity then usually falls after childhood. This alone does not prove lactose intolerance: other persistence alleles exist, the African ones of the rows below among them, and this table does not hold every one.

column10: Two copies of -13910T: lactase activity usually stays into adulthood.
column12: Lactase persistence is dominant: one copy of a persistence allele is usually enough. -13910T explains it in Europeans; in Africa and the Middle East other alleles do (rows -14010, -13915, -13907 and -14009). These rows hold the main known persistence alleles, not every one, so a genotype with none of them does not prove lactase non-persistence.

column9: C/T: 32% of people with this genotype in the study sneezed in bright light.
column10: T/T: 28% of people with this genotype in the study sneezed in bright light.

column10: Two T copies: freckles, sun-sensitive skin and brown rather than blond hair are more likely.

column7: Red hair and fair skin (MC1R R151C)
column8: No R151C.
column9: One R151C copy, a red-hair variant of MC1R. Red hair usually needs a variant on both copies, but in a British study one R151C copy already raised the chance of red hair, and one variant copy went with skin that burns more easily and with freckles: averages of the people studied, not a prediction for you.
column10: Two R151C copies: red hair and fair skin that tans poorly are likely.
column12: Red hair usually needs a red-hair MC1R variant on both copies of the gene: the same one twice, or two different ones (rows rs1805007, rs1805008, rs1805009). One copy at two of these rows can mean one on each copy; the phase is not known here. In a study of red-haired British families and unrelated people (Flanagan 2000), red hair was usually recessive and the effect grew with the number of variant copies. These are findings of the people studied, not rules: MC1R variants are not always enough for red hair (in a study of 25 red-haired and 62 other twins, some twin pairs with the same MC1R alleles differed in hair colour), and some red-haired people carry only one variant copy, or other MC1R variants than these three.

column7: MTHFR enzyme activity (C677T), an enzyme note, not health advice
column8: 677C on both copies: the usual MTHFR enzyme.
column9: One 677T copy: in lab tests the enzyme is somewhat less active and less stable to heat. This is common and is no reason to change diet or supplements.
column10: 677T on both copies: in lab tests lower MTHFR activity and, on average, somewhat higher blood homocysteine. It is not a diagnosis and no reason for treatment.
column12: Common (about 38% of chromosomes in the original study carry 677T). The American College of Medical Genetics found too little evidence for MTHFR testing and advises against it in the work-up of thrombophilia or recurrent pregnancy loss, and for relatives of a carrier (Hickey et al. 2013).

column8: No copy of the W143X stop: a secretor, with blood group antigens in saliva and other body fluids, unless another FUT2 variant, not read here, stops the gene.
column9: One W143X copy: a secretor, since one working FUT2 copy is enough, unless the other copy carries another FUT2 variant, not read here.
column10: Non-secretor: no blood group antigens in saliva. About 20% of the people the original study typed had this genotype. In a challenge study nobody with this genotype was infected by Norwalk virus.
column12: The stop codon is W143X in the original numbering (c.461G>A, often written c.428G>A). How common it is differs between populations, and in some, other FUT2 alleles, weak secretor alleles among them, are the common ones; they are not read here. Step 41 (blood groups, opt-in with TOOLS=...,bloodtype) reads more FUT2 null alleles; weak secretor alleles are not read there either.

column8: No copy of the G allele linked to lower vitamin D.
column9: One G copy: on average lower 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
column10: Two G copies: on average the lowest 25-hydroxyvitamin D (in the Framingham Heart Study cohort 64.6 against 82.6 nmol/L for T/T).
column12: A genome-wide study of 33,996 people of European descent. In its Framingham Heart Study cohort the mean was 82.6 nmol/L with T/T and 64.6 with G/G, against 83.4 and 74.7 with and without vitamin D supplements, and 61.6 in winter, 77.4 in spring and autumn and 95.8 in summer; the study calls the genotype gaps comparable to those of supplements and nearly as large as one change of season. In its discovery cohorts the variants at the three loci it confirmed explained up to 1 to 4% of the differences between people.

column7: Bilirubin level (UGT1A1, a Gilbert syndrome marker)
column8: No copy of the T allele.
column9: One T copy. In the bilirubin studies each T copy went with a higher bilirubin level on average; the UK Biobank study counted only two T copies as the genotype of Gilbert syndrome.
column10: Two T copies: the genotype a UK Biobank study used for Gilbert syndrome (about 10% of its participants), with higher bilirubin. Only 3% of people with it had the diagnosis recorded. A marker, not a diagnosis.
column12: rs887829 T is UGT1A1*80 (c.-364C>T). In people of European ancestry it travels with *28, the extra TA repeat of the UGT1A1 promoter that lowers the enzyme and is the common cause of Gilbert syndrome there: the UK Biobank study calls the two in complete linkage disequilibrium. Both studies were of people of European ancestry; in other populations the link and the common Gilbert alleles can differ. Other UGT1A1 variants are not read here. With STR_EXTRA_LOCI=yes, step 09 reads the UGT1A1 promoter TA repeat (*28) itself. Step 07 (PharmCAT) reports UGT1A1 for drugs.

column8: No CYP2A6*2 (Leu160His).
column9: One CYP2A6*2 copy: that copy makes an inactive enzyme.
column10: T/T at this site: two CYP2A6*2 copies, or one *2 copy with the other copy of the gene deleted (*4), which reads the same here. This row cannot tell the two apart, and it cannot say how fast nicotine is cleared: step 32 (pypgx) calls the CYP2A6 diplotype and copy number from the BAM.
column12: CYP2A6*2 is rare (1 to 3% in Finnish, Spanish and Swedish people). Other CYP2A6 alleles, deletions included, are not read here; step 32 (pypgx) calls CYP2A6 from the BAM.

column8: No copy of the G allele linked to a high Lp(a) level.
column9: One G copy: in the study it went with a higher Lp(a) level and coronary disease (odds ratio 1.70).
column10: Two G copies: a higher Lp(a) level is likely; in the study the G allele went with coronary disease (odds ratio 1.70).
column12: Lp(a) is a mostly inherited risk factor for coronary disease. With the other LPA row: one risk allele at either went with an odds ratio of 1.51 for coronary disease, two or more with 2.57, and both alleles went with a smaller apo(a) (fewer KIV-2 repeats; step 46 counts them). Studied in people of European descent; a sequencing study found partly different genetic determinants of Lp(a) in people of African ancestry. The actionable test is a blood Lp(a) measurement: a 2022 European Atherosclerosis Society consensus advises measuring it at least once in every adult.

column7: CFTR R117H, read with the CFTR poly-T tract
column8: No R117H copy.
column9: One R117H copy (Arg117His). What it means depends on the poly-T tract on the same copy: read it with the CFTR TG and poly-T line of the repeat expansions (step 09, STR_EXTRA_LOCI=yes).
column10: Two R117H copies (Arg117His). What they mean depends on the poly-T tracts: read them with the CFTR TG and poly-T line of the repeat expansions (step 09, STR_EXTRA_LOCI=yes).
